title: Wildfire victim trying to buy new Flin Flon, Man., home loses $170K in lawyer impersonation scam
summary: Five Manitobans in the last two months have fallen victim to a fraud scheme where scammers infiltrate lawyers' emails and redirect money. One woman in Flin Flon, trying to buy a new home after losing…

image.caption: Lisa Holmes sits in her parents' home in Flin Flon, Man., where she's lived since her home in nearby Denare Beach, Sask., was destroyed in a 2025 fire. She tried to buy a home of her own in Flin Flon earlier this year, but fell victim to an online scam and lost over $170,000. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

Five Manitobans in the last two months have fallen victim to a fraud scheme where scammers infiltrate lawyers' emails and redirect money. One woman in Flin Flon, trying to buy a new home after losing hers in a wildfire, is out more than $170,000.
Nearly $1M lost in 5 cases in recent months targeting lawyers and clients: Law Society of Manitoba

A Flin Flon woman whose home was destroyed in a wildfire has lost tens of thousands of dollars after falling prey to an online impersonation scam — one that has cost Manitobans nearly $1 million in just two months.

She was one of several people targeted recently by what the Manitoba Law Society calls a "payment misdirection fraud," where a scammer pretends to be a person's lawyer, orchestrates a large payment, then takes the money, often leaving the victim with little recourse to recover it.

Lisa Holmes was living in the northeastern Saskatchewan community of Denare Beach, about 20 kilometres southwest of Flin Flon, when a forest fire hit the area in June 2025. Her home and possessions were destroyed.
Holmes had limited insurance coverage and couldn't fully rebuild, so she moved in with her parents while trying to buy a new house.
The remains of Lisa Holmes's house in Denare Beach, Sask., which was destroyed by a wildfire on June 2, 2025. (Submitted by Lisa Holmes)

She found one for sale in Flin Flon and began working with a lawyer, Dayna Zaharia in The Pas, Man., to buy it. They communicated through email and used the online Docusign service for contract signatures, Holmes said.

She was instructed to send a wire transfer for more than $170,000 to a bank account, where it would be held until the sale was finalized, and sent that transfer through Flin Flon's RBC branch on Oct. 5, she said.
But she wasn't messaging Zaharia about that transfer — it was a scammer impersonating the lawyer.

"I didn't find out until a few days into it that the email was hacked," said Holmes. "Someone was impersonating myself and my lawyer and they were sending emails to one another, but we didn't know … until after we talked."
By then, the money was gone. Holmes didn't get the house. She's still living with her parents and worried she'll never get her money back.
"I was so excited that I was going to get my home. I never thought I was going to be blindsided like that."
Bank says client responsible
Holmes said she and Zaharia contacted the Law Society of Manitoba, which says they were targeted in a growing wave of payment misdirection fraud.
Zaharia declined an interview request, citing attorney-client privilege. Law society representatives also declined, saying they do not publicly comment on individual cases.
The regulatory body issued a statement Nov. 18, saying it's aware of five cases of "payment misdirection" fraud in Manitoba in the past two months alone, with almost $1 million lost.

The law society said scammers use the "infiltrated" accounts of lawyers or employees to send an email to another lawyer's client, a financial institution or a third party, telling them to send funds to a bank account that's actually controlled by the fraudster.

In most of the recent cases, it appears there was no insurance, the statement said. The scams went beyond real estate transactions, and two cases involved law firms that don't even have trust accounts.
RBC says as scams become more sophisticated, people should independently verify banking information before sending money. (David Donnelly/CBC)
Holmes notified RBC Nov. 4, filing a complaint stating it failed to protect her from financial abuse.
In an email response Holmes shared with CBC, the bank maintained she is "held responsible due to participation in fraud or scam," and said it considers the matter closed.
In a statement to CBC, an RBC spokesperson said as scams become more sophisticated, people should independently verify banking information before sending money.

blocks.text: The bank said it provides information about fraud prevention on its website, as does the Canadian Anti-Scam Coalition, which RBC is part of.
"You wonder, how does this happen? How does someone just steal over $170,000 and there's no accountability?" said Holmes.
"It would be so simple for the bank to just do a second check, right?"
Preventative steps
Holmes contacted the RCMP, who said they are investigating hers and similar cases.
Cpl. Ricky Perkins, who works with the Manitoba RCMP's cyber and financial crime unit, says they often see scams begin with clicking a link in a phishing email.
Scammers will "infiltrate the system" and set up rules in email programs like Outlook or Gmail, he said.
"Then they'll monitor the activity to see kind of who's who in the zoo … [and] take over the account."
Cpl. Ricky Perkins works with Manitoba RCMP's cyber and financial crime unit. He says scams like these are becoming more frequent and more sophisticated. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)
He said there are email precautions people can take to avoid being hacked, including checking sent and trash folders for any sent emails that don't look familiar.
"That would be a really good indicator that the account's been breached," he said.

The law society also advises lawyers to check their email folders for suspicious activity. It also says they should tell clients they won't accept or change payment instructions by email, and should confirm any payment information by phone.

items: Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back

blocks.text: If people are targeted in a scam, they can try to cancel or reverse the payment through their bank or contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, said Cpl. Perkins.
"Every case is different. In some cases we have recovered funds. In other cases, unfortunately, we can't," he said.

"There have been instances where people have been charged, and then obviously there's cases where the funds do end up in kind of the multiverse, so to speak. It's a difficult path for us to continue to follow."

Holmes holds one of the few things left after her Denare Beach home burned down in 2025 — a school art project she made as a child, with her handprint pressed onto plaster. She hopes RCMP will catch the person who scammed her. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)
RCMP said no arrests have been made in Holmes's case.
She said she hopes she'll recover her money and buy a new home, but if the bank and insurance can't help, she hopes the Mounties get their culprit — and that person will pay.
"[The courts] can tell them to pay it back if they have the money, but they also tell me that could take years," she said.
"I have a little bit of hope, but I don't have a lot of hope."
